div.p: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities via large-scale reinforcement learning (RL). However, leveraging the RL algorithm to empower effective multi-tool collaborative reasoning in LLMs remains an open challenge. In this paper, we introduce Tool-Star, an RL-based framework designed to empower LLMs to autonomously invoke multiple external tools during stepwise reasoning. Tool-Star integrates six types of tools and incorporates systematic designs in both data synthesis and training. To address the scarcity of tool-use data, we propose a general tool-integrated reasoning data synthesis pipeline, which combines tool-integrated prompting with hint-based sampling to automatically and scalably generate tool-use trajectories. A subsequent quality normalization and difficulty-aware classification process filters out low-quality samples and organizes the dataset from easy to hard. Furthermore, we propose a two-stage training framework to enhance multi-tool collaborative reasoning by: (1) cold-start fine-tuning, which guides LLMs to explore reasoning patterns via toolinvocation feedback; and (2) a multi-tool self-critic RL algorithm with hierarchical reward design, which reinforces reward understanding and promotes effective tool collaboration. Experimental analyses on over 10 challenging reasoning benchmarks highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of Tool-Star. The code is available at https://github.com/dongguanting/Tool-Star.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities empowered by large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) [59,21,57,36,79]. Advanced models exemplified by Deepseek R1 [9] and OpenAI o1 [41] exhibit diverse emergent behaviors in Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, including deep thinking, self-reflection, thereby improving problem-solving performance on complex reasoning tasks [48,40]. However, real-world reasoning scenarios often require models to integrate multiple capabilities through interaction with the environment, such as deep information seeking, long-term knowledge memory, and precise computation. To achieve this, Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) [17,28,67,72,42] approaches encourage LLMs to interact with external tools during the reasoning process, substantially expanding the paradigm from language-only reasoning to a broader scope of applications.

Current foundational work on TIR primarily focuses on distilling tool-use trajectories from strong models and applying supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to guide weaker models via imitation learning [17,27,76,22]. As large reasoning models exhibit emergent capabilities, subsequent efforts aim to enhance long chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs through tool-integrated prompting design [2,30,31,69,62]. However, these approaches rarely enable LLMs to autonomously discover effective reasoning patterns of tool usage. To address this limitation, recent studies introduce outcome-based rewards [4,51], extending reinforcement learning to the TIR domain [53,23,1,16,35,64,46]. While RL-based methods encourage exploration of efficient tool-use behaviors, they primarily focus on interacting with the individual tool. Notably, real-world reasoning tasks often require LLMs to possess both accurate computation and dynamic information-seeking capabilities. 2 This necessitates deeper integration of feedback from multiple tools, particularly search engines and code generators. The lack of systematic investigation into multi-tool collaborative reasoning presents a major bottleneck for practical TIR deployment. In this work, we aim to bridge this gap by addressing the following research questions:

1. Rationality and efficiency of tool usage. How to enable the model to perform efficient toolaugmented reasoning while balancing the cost of tool invocation. 2. Multi-tool collaborative reasoning. How to effectively enable models to integrate the functionalities of multiple tools throughout the reasoning process.

In this paper, we propose Tool-Star, a reinforcement learning-based framework designed to empower LLMs to autonomously invoke multiple external tools during stepwise reasoning. Specifically, Tool-Star integrates six types of tools into the reasoning process (three for training and three for inference-time optimization) and incorporates systematic designs in both data synthesis and training algorithms.

To address the scarcity of tool-use data, we first design a general Tool-Integrated Reasoning Data Synthesis Pipeline that combines tool-integrated prompting with hint-based sampling to automatically generate large-scale tool-use trajectories. We then introduce a quality normalization and difficulty-aware classification process to effectively filter out unreasonable tool-use samples and partition the data in a curriculum-like manner from easy to hard [54,11,12]. Leveraging this pipeline, we construct high-quality datasets for both cold-start fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a staged manner, laying a solid foundation for subsequent TIR training.

To incentivize the model's capability for multi-tool collaboration, we propose a two-stage TIR training framework that progressively aligns reasoning abilities in an easy-to-hard manner. (1) In the first stage, we introduce a Cold-Start Supervised Fine-Tuning strategy, allowing LLMs to initially explore reasoning patterns with feedback from tool invoking. (2) In the second stage, we develop a Multi-Tool Self-Critic Reinforcement Learning Algorithm. Unlike prior RL approaches that focus on single-tool usage, our method employs a hierarchical reward mechanism that not only evaluates answer correctness and tool-use format but also assigns additional rewards for effective multi-tool collaboration. To further improve the model's understanding of this complex reward structure, we interleave a self-critic reward fine-tuning phase within the standard RL process, facilitating the internalization of reward principles.

To comprehensively evaluate the capability of Tool-Star, we design experiments across more than 10 challenging computational reasoning tasks (e.g., AIME24 and MATH500 [37]) and knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks (e.g., WebWalker [68] and HotpotQA [73]). As illustrated in Figure 1, Tool-Star demonstrates strong overall reasoning performance while ensuring both efficiency and reliability in tool usage. In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

• We propose Tool-Star, a two-stage training framework to enhance multi-tool collaborative reasoning in LLMs: (1) Cold-Start fine-tuning enables LLMs to explore reasoning patterns guided by toolinvocation feedback; (2) Multi-Tool self-critic RL algorithm with a hierarchical reward design reinforces the LLM's grasp of reward principles and promotes effective multi-tool collaboration.

• To address the scarcity of tool-use data, we propose a general TIR data synthesis pipeline that combines tool-integrated prompting with hint-based sampling to automatically and scalably generate tool-use trajectories. We further introduce a quality normalization and difficulty-aware classification process to filter out unreasonable samples and organize the dataset from easy to hard.
• Experiments on more than 10 challenging reasoning datasets validate the effectiveness of Tool-Star.
Further quantitative analyses demonstrate its high efficiency, offering insights for incentivizing multi-tool collaborative reasoning.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Tool-Integrated Reasoning. Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing LLM reasoning by enabling autonomous invocation of external tools. Existing TIR approaches can be broadly categorized into three streams: (1) Prompting-based methods guide models to use tools via carefully crafted prompts without additional training [2,30,38,31,69,25,62]. While easy to implement, they often suffer from instability and limited accuracy in tool usage. (2) SFT-based methods apply supervised fine-tuning to teach weaker models tool use by distilling trajectories from stronger models [17,27,76,22,33,10,13,28]. Though effective, their performance is constrained by the quality of demonstrations and limited generalization beyond seen examples. (3) RLbased methods optimize tool-use behavior via outcome-driven rewards [53,56,23,1,16,35,32,52], enabling models to autonomously discover effective tool-use strategies through exploration. This often leads to more robust and adaptive tool utilization than imitation-based approaches. Despite these advances, most work focuses on single-tool settings. Multi-tool collaborative reasoning-requiring coordination across heterogeneous tools (e.g., search engines, code interpreters)-remains underexplored. While systems like OTC [64] and ToolRL [45] have made initial progress, there is still a significant gap in developing specialized RL algorithms and reward mechanisms tailored for multi-tool collaboration.

Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have significantly enhanced reasoning capabilities in language models. Large-scale RL implementations such as DeepSeek-R1 [9], OpenAI-o1 [41], and QwQ [60] have demonstrated the effectiveness of RL for improving reasoning performance. Concurrently, several studies have explored achieving emergent reasoning capabilities with minimal resources, either through high-quality but small-scale datasets or smaller parameter models [79,74,34]. Notable examples include SimpleRL-Zoo [79], LIMO [74], LIMR [34], and Qwen's mathematical reasoning approach [71], with additional insights from works examining RL effectiveness in both small [7] and large models with minimal examples [66].

A series of research has focused on analyzing RL training strategies and reward function design for reasoning tasks, providing practical insights for broader applications. Key contributions include PRIME [6], which explores process reinforcement through implicit rewards, empirical studies on improving R1-like reasoning models [3,75], and DAPO's scalable RL system [77]. Another research direction has concentrated on optimizing reasoning efficiency through specialized RL algorithms, as demonstrated in works on concise reasoning [15,47,55]. More recently, researchers have begun integrating external tools to enhance reasoning accuracy, with notable examples including ToRL [35], ReTool [16], ToolRL [46], and OTC [64]. However, exploration of multi-tool collaborative reasoning remains relatively limited, highlighting a significant gap in current research.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: Tool-Star is an RL-based framework that empowers LLMs to autonomously invoke multiple external tools during reasoning. As shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3, Tool-Star includes two key components: (1) A tool-integrated data synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale, high-quality reasoning trajectories with reasonable tool usage ( §3.1); (2) A two-stage training paradigm that facilitates multi-tool collaborative reasoning, comprising cold-start fine-tuning and a multi-tool self-critic RL algorithm ( §3.2). We delve into the specifics of our approach as follows.

Problem Formulation. Multi-tool Collaborative Reasoning aims to enable LLMs to perform multistep reasoning through interaction and collaboration with multiple external tools. Specifically, given a task query q and an external tool set T , Tool-Star autonomously invokes tools during the generation of the reasoning chain R c , guided by the tool-integrated instruction I T . The real-time tool-call feedback F T is dynamically concatenated into the reasoning chain to facilitate ongoing inference until the final output y is produced. This process can be modeled as:
div.formula: P θ (R c , y | IT , q, T ) = Tc t=1 P θ (R c t | R c <t , I T , q, {F T }<t) Multi-Tool Integrated Reasoning • Ty t=1 P θ (yt | y<t, Rc, I T , q) Answer Generation ,(1)
div.p: where T c denotes the number of tokens in the reasoning chain R c , R c t is the token at position t, and R c <t represents all tokens generated before t. {F T } <t denotes the feedback of all tool calls prior to t. T y is the length of the Answer y, with y t as the token at position t.

div.head: Tool Design.
div.p: In this work, we design six tools to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs within the Tool-Star framework. During the two-stage training process, we introduce three core tools that enable LLMs to autonomously invoke external functionalities during reasoning:
• Search Engine: Executes search queries to retrieve relevant information, supporting both local and web-based search modes.
• Web Browser Agent: Parses web search results by visiting URLs, extracting relevant content, and
summarizing key information in response to the query.
• Code Interpreter: Executes code snippets generated by the LLM in a sandbox environment, returning either the execution results or error messages based on code correctness.
During inference, we introduce three Inference-time tools to optimize the reliability of TIR process:
• Code Debugger: Automatically corrects LLM-generated erroneous code by leveraging the original code and compiler error messages to guide revisions.
• Tool-Use Backtracer: Locates and rolls back to the reasoning step preceding a failed tool invocation, enabling the model to resume and revise its reasoning path.

• Reasoning Chain Refiner: When the output exceeds the maximum length, refiner prunes and optimizes redundant steps in the reasoning process, replacing original reasoning chain with a more concise and coherent version to complete the task.

div.head: Tool-Integrated Reasoning Data Synthesis
div.p: In this section, we present our tool-integrated reasoning data synthesis pipeline, aiming to enable automated and scalable construction of high-quality tool-use datasets (Figure 2).

div.head: Step-1: Data Collection and Sampling
div.p: To balance data scale and diversity while ensuring accessibility, we curate a high-quality training set from open-source knowledge-based and computational reasoning datasets, comprising approximately 90K text-based reasoning data (D text ) and 1K existing TIR datasets (D tool ), as summarized in Table 5.
To further expand TIR trajectories, we introduce two complementary sampling strategies:

(1) TIR Prompting-based Sampling. We design a tool-integrated prompt I T to guide the LLM P θ in sampling responses for queries in D text . Following the Eq.( 2), LLM decodes tool-invoking requests within special tokens (e.g., <search> ... </search> , <python> ... </python> ) during trajectory generation. We then automatically parse and extract these requests, invoke external tools to obtain feedback F , and insert the tool feedback-enclosed within <result> and </result> tags-back into the reasoning chain as additional context for subsequent generation steps. This process iterates until either (1) the maximum number of tool calls or length is reached, or (2) the model generates a final answer, enclosed by designated tokens <answer> and </answer> . After inference on the entire D text , we filter for correct samples to obtain the dataset D P tool . (2) Hint-based Sampling. To further diversify tool invoking patterns, we employ a hint-based method [29] that inserts hint tool-call tokens into language-only reasoning trajectories. We first prompt the LLM to perform language-only reasoning on queries from D text . Following the START [28], we propose two hint instructions-Logical Verification and Answer Reflection-to insert tool-invoking hints into the original reasoning chains. As shown in Figure 2, logical verification hints randomly replace uncertain expressions (e.g., maybe, wait, not sure) in the chain, while reflection hints are inserted after the answer. These diverse hints facilitate the model to invoke tools when information is insufficient or after answer generation, enabling information completion and answer verification. After inserting hints, we truncate the original reasoning chain at the hint position, prompting the model to perform tool-augmented reasoning in response to the hint, which can be formulated as:
div.formula: P θ (R c >t H , y | IT , q, R c ≤t H , T ) = Tc t=t H P θ (R c t | R c ≤t , I T , q, {F T } ≤t ) Hint-based Tool-Integrated Reasoning • Ty t=1 P θ (yt | y<t, Rc, I T , q) Answer Generation ,(2)
div.p: Unlike Eq.( 2), t H is the end position of the hint insertion, and R c ≤t represents the language-only reasoning chain before the hint position. The LLM continues reasoning from R c ≤t with q to derive the tool-integrated reasoning chain R c >t H . Other variables are defined consistently with Eq.( 2). After filtering the samples for the correct answers, we obtain the hint-based TIR dataset D H tool . Finally, we merge two datasets to obtain the final dataset D v1 tool = {D H tool ∪ D M tool ∪ D tool }.

div.head: Step-2: Tool-Use Quality Normalization.
div.p: To ensure the rationality of tool usage within each sample, we implement the following 3 TIR normalization strategies for tool-use data quality control: (1) Tool-call Frequency Control: Remove samples with tool-call frequency exceeding a predefined threshold β to alleviate excessive tool invocation.
(2) Duplicate Tool-call Removal: Eliminate samples containing redundant tool calls, such as repeated generation of identical search queries or code snippets in the same response.

(3) Format Normalization: Standardize tool call formats in reasoning chains by unifying special tokens for invocation, feedback, and final answers, while ensuring balanced usage of start and end tokens. By applying these criteria, we obtain a quality-filtered dataset denoted as D v2 tool .

div.head: Step-3: Difficulty-Aware Data Classification.
div.p: Considering the computational overhead of tool-use and the multi-stage nature of TIR training, we argue that a high-quality tool-use dataset should meet the following criteria: (1) Invoke tools only when necessary: Tool calls should be avoided when the model is capable of solving the problem through direct reasoning.
(2) Organize samples from easy to hard: As emphasized in prior RL tool learning [53,81], stage-wise training based on sample difficulty is crucial for effective learning.

To achieve the above objectives, we first perform a language-only reasoning pass on each question in the dataset D v2 tool , yielding a direct reasoning result denoted as D v2 text . Based on the correctness of both direct reasoning (DR) and tool-integrated reasoning (TIR), each sample is categorized into four types (Figure 2). For categories 1 and 2, where the model already produces correct answers through direct reasoning, tool use is deemed unnecessary. These samples are extracted from D v2 text to form a subset D sub text . For category 3, which clearly illustrates the advantages of tool use over language-only reasoning, we directly sample from D v2 tool to construct the subset D sub tool . To support a curriculum learning paradigm [11] from easy to hard, we construct a cold-start finetuning dataset D SFT tool by combining D sub text and D sub tool . For Category-4 samples, which are challenging for both DR and TIR, are treated as hard examples and reserved for reinforcement learning, forming the dataset D RL tool . This design enables the LLM to acquire basic tool-use capabilities through coldstart fine-tuning, and subsequently generalize to more complex scenarios during the RL phase (e.g. multi-tool collaboration), thereby facilitating a progressive learning trajectory.

div.head: Tool-Star: A Two-stage Multi-tool Collaborative Training Framework
div.p: In this section, we propose a two-stage multi-tool collaborative training framework that generalize the LLM's TIR capability from a single to multiple tool-use paradigm, and from easy to hard learning.

div.head: Cold-Start Supervised Fine-tuning.
div.p: To equip the LLM with an initial understanding of tool usage for problem solving, given (x i , y i ) ∈ D SFT tool , we apply the standard Supervised Fine-tuning objective on the backbone model P θ with parameters θ: L(θ) = -(xi,yi)∈D SFT tool log P θ (y i | x i ) , where x i denotes the i-th input. Ultimately, we obtain a cold-start LLM πθ with initial TIR capability.
Multi-Tool Self-Critic Reinforcement Learning. We will introduce how the LLM learn to autonomously invoke tools, including a Code interpreter, a search engine and a web browser agent.

(1) Memory-based Roll-Out with Tools. As shown in Figure 3, we employ multi-tool invocation instructions to guide the model in decoding tool-use requests into special tokens (e.g., <python> ) during the roll-out process. Upon detecting these tokens, the corresponding tool is automatically invoked, and the resulting feedback is integrated back into the reasoning chain. To reduce latency caused by frequent tool calls, we incorporate a memory mechanism that caches the mapping between each tool request and its output. This allows the model to retrieve responses for repeated requests directly from memory, thereby improving efficiency.

(2) Hierarchical Reward Design. Reward signals serve as the optimization objective and directly guide the behavior of the policy model during training. Distinct from previous tool-use RL approaches, we not only design correctness and format rewards for LLMs, but also introduce multi-tool collaborative rewards. This design aims to encourage multiple tool usage while maintaining LLM correctness. Specifically, when both the answer and tool invocation format are correct, and the model employs multiple tools (i.e., both <search> and <python> appear in the reasoning chain), an extra reward r M is granted. div.head: Multi-tool Collaborative Inference
div.p: During inference, we follow Eq.( 2), enabling the model to autonomously use the search engine, web browser agent, and Python interpreter. To improve TIR robustness, we introduce three inference-time mechanisms targeting common failure scenarios:
• Code Execution Error: When generated code contains syntax errors, the Code Debugger uses compiler messages and the original code to produce executable fixes.
• Tool Invocation Failure: If tool calls yield no useful output or debugging fails, the Backtracer identifies the statement before the tool-invoking token and restarts inference from there.

• Inference Length Overflow: When tool outputs exceed the context limit, the Chain Refiner compresses and restructures the reasoning chain by removing redundant or irrelevant content, allowing continued inference without tools.
These mechanisms enhance tool invocation reliability and provide an effective inference-time scaling strategy. Further details are listed in the Appendix B.2.

div.head: Datasets.
div.p: To comprehensively evaluate the tool-use capabilities of our model, we conduct experiments on two types of reasoning datasets: (1) Math reasoning benchmarks, including AIME2024, AIME2025foot_1 , MATH500 [37], MATH [18], and GSM8K. (2) Knowledge reasoning benchmarks, including three complex reasoning QA tasks: GAIA [39], HLE [43], and WebWalker [68]; and three Wikipedia-based open-domain QA tasks: HotpotQA [73], 2WikiMultihopQA [19], and Musique [63]. For all tasks, we follow previous work [31] and extract answers from the model output enclosed in \box{}.

Evaluation Metrics. For computational reasoning tasks, we follow Search-o1 [31] employ LLMbased judging (Qwen2.5-72B=Instruct) to ensure answer correctness. For open-domain QA tasks, we adopt token-level F1 score as the evaluation metric. To assess tool usage efficiency, we propose the Tool-use Efficiency metric:
div.formula: T E = 1 N N i=1 Si T c i
div.p: where N is the number of datasets, S i and T c i denote the number of correct answers and the number of total samples for the i-th dataset when using tools.

div.head: Baselines.
div.p: Our experiments include the following three categories of baselines: (1) Proprietary Models: Qwen2.5 [49], Llama3.2 [14]. (2) Single-tool Enhanced Baselines: Code-enhanced models such as ToRL [35] and DotaMath [27], and search-enhanced models such as Vanilla RAG [26], Search-o1 [31] and Search-R1 [23]. (3) Multi-tool Enhanced Baselines: Multiple tools integrated prompting and ReCall [1]. More details of implementations are provided in the Appendix C.

div.head: Results on Challenging Reasoning Tasks
div.p: Our main results are presented in Table 1. Overall, Tool-Star consistently outperforms all baselines, decisively establishing the superiority. Furthermore, we have identified the following insights:

(1) TIR prompting fails to explore the better tool-use behavior. Focusing on Search-o1 and Multi-Tool Prompting, their performance on comprehensive reasoning tasks remains suboptimal. Notably, multi-tool prompting strategies even exhibit lower consistency compared to their backbone model. This reveals that relying solely on prompt engineering to elicit tool usage is insufficient for guiding the LLM toward effective tool utilization, thereby limiting its reasoning capabilities.

(2) Single-tool RL-based methods exhibit strong domain specialization but limited generalizability. Search-enhanced RL approaches perform well on knowledge-intensive tasks (e.g., 40+% F1 on HQA), but their accuracy drops sharply by over 20% on computation-heavy tasks like MATH500 and AIME24 compared to the backbone model. Conversely, code-assistant methods like ToRL underperform on knowledge-based tasks, even falling behind RAG baselines. These trends underscore the specialization bias of single-tool RL methods and their limited cross-domain transferability.

(3) Tool-Star demonstrates strong and versatile reasoning, along with robust plug-and-play capability. Tool-Star consistently outperforms both single-and multi-tool baselines, achieving over 40% average accuracy across 10 datasets while maintaining competitive performance on individual tasks. Notably, it also delivers substantial gains across different backbone models, with average improvements nearing 20% on both Qwen and LLaMA. These results highlight Tool-Star's generality, efficiency, and strong adaptability across models and tasks. To further validate Tool-Star's generalizability, we present results on deep web exploration and a case study in Appendix A.1 and E.

div.head: HQA
div.p: Ablation Study. In this section, we conduct a systematic ablation study in Table 2, where "w/o" denotes removing a specific component. The results demonstrate that: (1) Removing any single module leads to performance degradation, highlighting the critical role of each part of design. (2) Excluding either results in significant performance drops. the Cold-Start phase helps the model initially acquire tooluse capabilities, while the RL phase promotes generalization in multi-tool reasoning. Both stages are indispensable and complementary. (3) Incorporating hierarchical rewards and a selfcritic mechanism on top of vanilla RL consistently brings further improvements, confirming the effectiveness of our tailored RL strategy.

div.head: Tool-Use Efficiency Analysis.
div.p: To validate whether Tool-Star can efficiently invoke tools during stepwise reasoning, we compare the Tool-use Accuracy T E of various TIR methods on knowledgeintensive and computation-based reasoning datasets, as shown in Figure 4 (left). Results indicate that while Search-R1 and ToRL achieve high accuracy in knowledge and computation tasks respectively, they underperform in the other domain-highlighting the tendency of single-tool RL methods to specialize in specific reasoning types. In contrast, Tool-Star consistently maintains high tool-use accuracy across both task types and baselines, demonstrating its efficiency in tool utilization. Local Search VS. Web Search. Inspired by R1-Searcher [53] and DeepResearch [81], we further compared the differences between local search and web search of Tool-Star-3B in knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks. As shown in Figure 5, we found that after using web search, except for HotpotQA which did not show obvious improvement, the other three domains all demonstrated significant improvements, especially 2wiki (+13% F1) and Bamboogle (+8% F1). Regarding the above phenomena, we believe that the performance differences between the two mainly stem from: (1)The retrieval library of wiki is a subset of the web page corpus. Moreover, when combined with the browser agent for web page information, it can provide more accurate and concise information compared to wiki documents.
(2) We use the Bing API 4 for web search, and the retrieval models and strategies of their services perform better than the E5-base we deployed offline for local search.

div.head: Inference-Time Tool-Use Analysis.
div.p: To verify the effectiveness of inference-time tool design, we further analyze its impact on the performance of Tool-Star and DotaMath across two datasets. As shown in Figures 4 (middle) and (right), both models exhibit a notable reduction in tool-use errors during reasoning after applying inference-time tool optimizations, accompanied by significant performance improvements. These results not only underscore the detrimental effect of incorrect tool usage on reasoning accuracy, but also reinforces the motivation for incorporating inference-time tools. Notably, the performance gain for DotaMath is substantially larger than that for Tool-Star, with improvements exceeding 20% on GSM8K. This suggests that inference-time tools are particularly beneficial for models with weaker coding capabilities, while models with stronger coding proficiency, such as Tool-Star, naturally make fewer tool-related errors and thus have less room for improvement.

div.head: Scaling Analysis on Parameter Scales.
div.p: To investigate the effectiveness of Tool-Star across different parameter scales, we display the RL training curves of Qwen2.5 models with 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters in Figure 6. Our key observations are as follows: (1) All models achieve good reward scores at the beginning of training (step 0), benefiting from the cold-start SFT stage, which significantly reduces the exploration burden in early RL; (2) As training progresses, the average reward scores steadily improve across all model sizes, indicating that our self-critic RL framework further improve TIR capabilities on top of the cold-start initialization. (3) Notably, the average reward shows signs of emergent improvement around step 10, while no clear inflection point (i.e., "aha moment") is observed in response length. Instead, response lengths gradually stabilize, suggesting convergence toward optimized response patterns. More training details can be found in Appendix A.3.

div.head: Scaling Analysis on the RL Training Curve.
div.p: To better understand the training dynamics of the reinforcement learning process, we present the trends of KL penalty, average reward score, average response length, and validation score over the first 100 steps RL training (Figure 7). Our key observations are as follows:
• All metrics-including reward score, KL penalty, and validation score-increase steadily with training steps, indicating the stability of our self-critic RL training method.

• The initial reward scores of the 3B and 1.5B models are already above 0 (within a possible range of -1 to 1.1), with corresponding validation scores starting at approximately 0.375 and 0.29 respectively-substantially higher than the vanilla instruct model's score of below 0.15. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our cold-start strategy. In contrast to RL methods trained entirely from scratch [35,53,23], the cold-start approach endows the model with a baseline level of TIR capability from the outset, significantly reducing the need for extensive black-box exploration during the early stages of RL training. • After cold-start SFT, the reward score shows mild emergence within the first 0-20 steps, though less pronounced than in from-scratch RL (i.e., no sudden rise-and-drop). Similarly, the response length does not fluctuate sharply but gradually converges to a stable value, further supporting the stability benefits of cold-start training.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we introduce Tool-Star, an RL-based framework designed to enable LLMs to autonomously invoke multiple external tools during stepwise reasoning. To address the scarcity of tool-use data, Tool-Star employs a scalable TIR data synthesis pipeline, incorporating normalization and a difficulty-aware data classification process. Furthermore, we propose a two-stage training framework to enhance multi-tool collaborative reasoning in LLMs, consisting of a Cold-Start Finetuning phase and a Multi-Tool Self-Critic RL stage. This framework progressively fosters effective multi-tool collaboration and strengthens the LLM's understanding of reward principles. Extensive experiments across over ten challenging benchmarks demonstrate that Tool-Star significantly improves both the effectiveness and efficiency of tool-augmented reasoning in LLMs.

div.head: B.1 Training Algorithm of Tool-Star
div.p: In this section, we delve into the overall workflow of the our Multi-Tool Self-Critic Reinforcement Learning algorithm. The training process consists of two alternating phases over multiple cycles, which are illustrated in algorithm 1:

(1) Vanilla RL stage: In each cycle, the model π θ is first optimized via GRPO for a fixed number of steps. For each query sampled from the dataset, the task instruction is prepended, and the model generates multiple output sequences using external tools. These outputs are used to compute the GRPO objective (Eq. 4), and the model parameters are updated accordingly.

(2) Self-Critic DPO stage: After GRPO, a self-critic phase is performed to refine the model's decision-making. For each sampled query, the model generates multiple outputs, from which one preferred (correct) and one rejected (incorrect) response are selected. These are used to compute the DPO objective (Eq. 5), further updating the model via gradient ascent. This alternating training scheme enables the model to not only improve through reinforcement learning with tool-augmented outputs but also self-correct by distinguishing between good and bad generations. The final output is a tool-aware reasoning model π new θ optimized for both performance and efficiency.

The summarized output is then fed back into the reasoning chain. Notably, the browser agent is optional-when it is not used, the search engine directly returns webpage snippets or raw text.

• Code Interpreter: Code snippets generated by the language model are executed in a sandboxed environment, returning either the execution result or error messages based on correctness. Our Python interpreter implementation follows the design of ToRA [17], ensuring secure and accurate execution.
Inference-time tool:

• Code Debugger: This module automatically corrects erroneous code generated by large language models and guides the code revision process. Specifically, we design a dedicated debug prompt ( D.2) that incorporates the model-generated code and compiler error messages, enabling the model to understand and fix the errors for automated code correction.

• Tool-Use Backtracer: This module identifies and reverts to the reasoning step prior to a failed tool call, allowing the model to recover and revise its reasoning path. In real experiments, we compared model-based and rule-based rewinding strategies. As the model often struggles to accurately locate the faulty tool call, we adopt the rule-based approach. Concretely, we set the rewind position at the newline token preceding the special token of the erroneous tool call, prompting the model to regenerate the reasoning chain from that point.

• Reasoning Chain Refiner: When the model output exceeds the maximum length limit, this module prunes and refines redundant steps in the reasoning process, replacing the original chain with a more concise and coherent version to complete the task. div.p: In this section, we sample data from sources including Numina-MATH, 2Wiki, HotpotQA, with the detailed breakdown and corresponding data sizes presented in Table 5. We strictly adhere to all copyright and licensing terms associated with the datasets and open-source code.
For the computational reasoning dataset, we use 72.4K samples aligned with Numina-MATH TIR.

Finally, we obtained approximately 100K samples containing 1% TIR data.

It is important to note that we only use the queries from these language-only datasets for reasoning chain sampling, without relying on the reasoning chains generated by stronger models of original datasets. Our cold-start data is sampled using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, which serves as the backbone model to match the parameter scale of the main table. Following the START settings [28], we set the temperature to 0.7 and the top-p value to 0.95 during sampling. Due to resource constraints, each question is sampled three times only. In the tool-use quality normalization stage, our tool-call frequency threshold β is set to 5.

Ultimately, following multiple stages of quality filtering in Section 3.1, we curated approximately 54K samples from categories 1, 2, and 3 for cold-start training. Furthermore, 10K challenging samples were randomly selected from categories-4 samples for the RL phase to enable progressive alignment from simpler to more difficult tasks.

div.head: C.2 Training Details of Tool-Star
div.p: Cold-Start Supervised Finetuning. After applying our sampling strategies to the original datasets, we use approximately 54k samples for cold-start supervised fine-tuning. During the supervised fine-tuning stage, we fine-tune a Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model on the training data with a learning rate of 7e-6. We utilize DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 [50] and FlashAttention2 [8] for training. The batch size is set to 128, weight decay to 0.1, and we train for 3 epoch. Mixed precision training with BF16 is adopted, and the maximum input length is set to 4096.

Multi-Tool Self-Critic Reinforcement Learning. After SFT, we further train the model using the GRPO algorithm under the VERL framework 6 . Similarly, we randomly select around 10k samples from D RL tool for reinforcement learning. The learning rate is set to 8, with 8 rollouts per sample. The total training batch size is 128, and the mini-batch size is 16. The maximum output length is set to 4096 to ensure completeness of exploration. To accelerate the training speed, following DAPO [77], we set the maximum number of tool invocations during training to 3. To stabilize training, we set the KL divergence coefficient in GRPO to 0. The reinforcement learning phase lasts for 2 epochs. All experiments are conducted on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. To ensure reproducibility, all experimental results are averages of three independent trials. We have approximately 300 samples in the validation set during the RL stage, which includes AIME25, 25, MATH500, HotpotQA, 2wikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue and Bamboogle.

It is worth noting that all tool invocation results in Tool-Star are masked. As illustrated in the Figure 3, these masked segments are excluded from the loss computation to prevent the training policy from being biased toward the tool outputs. Only the tokens from the text-based reasoning process and tool requests are considered during loss calculation.

Self-Critic DPO Training. In this phase, the learning rate is set to 5e-7 with a cosine scheduler and a 0.1 warm-up ratio. We use DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 and Flash-Attention 2 for efficiency, with a global batch size of 64. Training utilizes a sigmoid loss function with a beta value of 0.3 and spans 2 epochs. Mixed precision training with bf16 is employed, and the maximum context length is 4096 tokens. We perform self-critic training every 0.5 epoch during the standard reinforcement learning process (approximately every 50 steps), and use the resulting model to resume the subsequent vanilla reinforcement learning training. The detailed data format are listed in Appendix E.2

div.head: C.4 Baseline Details Proprietary Models
div.p: • Qwen2.5 Series [70,49], developed by Alibaba, is available in several sizes: Qwen2.5-0.5B /1.5B /7B and 72B. This model is trained on data sources spanning 29 kinds of languages, enabling it to perform exceptionally well in multilingual tasks. Additionally, Qwen2.5 exhibits strong capabilities in coding and mathematics. Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct is notable for its ability to handle input windows of up to 128K tokens in length, making it exceptionally well-suited for processing long texts and tackling complex tasks.

• LLaMA 3 Series [14], developed by Meta AI, is released in multiple sub-series, including LLaMA 3, LLaMA 3.1, LLaMA 3.2 and LLaMA 3.3. LLaMA series models offer two primary variants for each model size: the base model and the instruct model. These models are trained on a mixture of datasets, covering a wide range of domains and languages. The LLaMA series models achieve strong performance across reasoning, coding, and multilingual understanding benchmarks.
With continued improvements in alignment and context length, they are increasingly suitable for real-world tasks.

div.head: Search-Enhanced Baselines
div.p: • RAG [26] is a basic baseline that demonstrates the model's ability to directly utilize retrieved information. In our implementation, we directly used the retriever to obtain the top-5 results and inserted them into a carefully designed prompt to let the model generate the answer.

• Search-o1 [31] is a reasoning-model-driven RAG method. Its core idea is to allow the reasoning model to autonomously decide whether to perform a search during its reasoning process. It generates queries, retrieves relevant information, organizes the retrieved results, and incorporates them into the model's reasoning chain. The model then continues generation based on this chain until a final answer is reached. In our experiments, we modified the official code of Search-o1 by replacing its base model with one that has the same number of parameters as ours, and we also used the same retriever to ensure consistency.

• Search-R1 [23] is a reinforcement learning method that trains a model from scratch to call the search engine during reasoning. Its overall process is similar to Search-o1 [31]: the model generates necessary queries during reasoning, retrieves relevant information, and inserts it into the reasoning chain. We follow the original prompt used in the method to ensure its effectiveness.

div.head: Code-Enhanced Baselines
div.p: • ToRL [35] is a tool-integrated framework trained with reinforcement learning methods. This framework enables the model to autonomously invoke code interpreter to solve mathematical reasoning problems. Compared to prompt-based methods and supervised fine-tuning training approaches, ToRL encourages the model to explore extensively to find optimal tool usage strategies. This approach shows significant improvements over traditional methods. At the same time, the framework demonstrates the broad potential applications of tool integration in mathematical reasoning.

• DotaMath [27] models are fine-tuned on mathematical instruction datasets. After training, the DotaMath model demonstrates strong capabilities in solving complex mathematical reasoning problems. By training on the DotaMathQA dataset built for mathematical problems, the model has acquired the abilities of thought decomposition and self-correction during reasoning. This paradigm opens up a new direction for solving complex math problems.

div.head: Multi-tool Enhanced Baselines
div.p: • Multi-Tool Prompting method refers to the approach where the model learns to use external tools to solve problems solely through prompts. In this setup, we primarily aim to explore whether the model has the capability to autonomously call relevant tools to complete tasks. For the prompt format, we use the same structure as the one employed by Tool-Star. The specific prompt can be found in Appendix D.1.

• ReCall [1] method makes significant improvements over the ReSearch framework. Specifically, compared to the purely search-based framework, it further allows the model to call code interpreter to solve complex reasoning problems. This setup expands the tasks that ReSearch could handle to mathematical reasoning, while still maintaining the original capability of ReSearch to call search engines. Additionally, ReCall introduces a new method for generating data towards complex multi-step tasks, enabling the LLM to develop sophisticated reasoning abilities based on multiple tools.

div.head: C.5 Datasets Details
div.p: We provide a detailed introduction to the computational reasoning benchmarks evaluated by Tool-Star:

• AIME24 7 A dataset of 30 challenging math problems from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME I & II), covering algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Each JSONL-formatted entry includes the problem ID, statement, detailed solution steps, and the final integer answer. Designed to evaluate large language models on complex mathematical reasoning, the dataset features high difficulty, rigorous multi-step solutions, and unique answers-making it a strong benchmark for assessing advanced problem-solving capabilities.

• AIME25foot_6 is a dataset comprising 30 challenging mathematical problems sourced from the 2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME I & II). These problems encompass a diverse range of topics, including algebra, combinatorics, geometry, number theory, and probability. AIME25 is designed to evaluate the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs. It serves as a benchmark for assessing how well these models can tackle complex mathematical problems requiring multi-step reasoning and understanding of advanced mathematical concepts.

• GSM8K [5] is a widely adopted benchmark for assessing the mathematical reasoning abilities of large language models through grade-school level word problems. In our experiments, we utilize its standard test set and report performance based on greedy decoding accuracy (maj@1).

• MATH [18] is a dataset consisting of challenging high school-level mathematics problems, spanning topics such as Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting & Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus. Compared to GSM8K, MATH offers greater difficulty and topic diversity.

• MATH500 [37] is a subset of 500 problems drawn from the MATH benchmark developed by OpenAI. This dataset is designed to assess the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. The problems in MATH500 cover a range of mathematical topics including algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and probability. Each entry in the dataset includes the problem statement, a detailed step-by-step solution, and the final answer, allowing for thorough model training and evaluation.
Furthermore, we also conduct a series experiments on follow knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks:

• WebWalker [68] s a dataset consisting of queries derived from various web pages, where answering a single query may require gathering information from one or multiple pages. In our experiments, we adopt an open-domain setting by using a search engine for retrieval rather than the root URLs provided in the dataset.
• HotPotQA [73] is a widely-used question answering dataset that features multi-hop questions built from Wikipedia articles. In our experiments, we use its validation set for evaluation.

• 2WikiMultihopQA [19] is a large-scale multi-hop QA dataset that combines structured knowledge from Wikidata and unstructured text from Wikipedia. It includes diverse question types and annotated reasoning paths to support explainable multi-step inference.

• Bamboogle [44] is a challenging multi-hop QA dataset that contains hand-crafted questions requiring up to four reasoning hops. It tests a model's ability to perform complex and compositional reasoning across multiple facts.

• Musique [63] is a multi hop dataset that requires inference. The problem inside is a dependency based multi hop problem, where one inference step depends on the information obtained from the previous inference step, making the dataset very difficult. We conducted experiments using Musique's dev set.

div.head: F Limitations and Future Directions
div.p: Despite our best efforts to optimize the overall Tool-Star pipeline, there remain certain limitations and areas for improvement that warrant further exploration.

• Expanding Tool Diversity: Currently, the Tool-Star framework integrates three tools during training and three tools during inference. Compared to prior work that relies on a single tool, our approach represents a pioneering and timely attempt. However, given the growing diversity of available tools, we believe many more remain to be explored for enhancing reasoning capabilities. For instance, incorporating vision-language models (VLMs) as external tools could further unlock visual understanding, and adopting the Model Context Protocol may enable more flexible tool invocation. We plan to continue expanding the types and integration of tools in future work, advancing multi-tool collaborative reasoning.

• Scaling Backbone Model Parameters: Due to limited computational resources and the timeconsuming rollout process in multi-tool reasoning, this work focuses on models with 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters for RL training and evaluation. Nonetheless, our "Scaling Analysis on Parameter Scales" (see Table 4) provides preliminary evidence of the Tool-Star framework's scalability. In future work, we aim to extend our experiments to larger models, such as 7B and 32B, to assess generalization across more complex tasks and model capacities.

Outlook: Achieving reliable and robust step-by-step reasoning remains a challenging task that demands continued research and innovation. We sincerely hope to collaborate with researchers in the fields of alignment and reasoning to jointly address these shared challenges and further advance tool-integrated reasoning systems.

div.head: G Broader Impacts
div.p: This study presents the Tool-Star framework, which empowers large language models with multi-tool collaborative reasoning, enhancing their adaptability and effectiveness in complex tasks. Through reinforcement learning and scalable data synthesis, Tool-Star offers a generalizable and flexible reasoning paradigm, demonstrating strong performance across benchmarks and broad potential in domains such as education, science, and engineering.

However, as models gain greater autonomy in tool use, concerns arise regarding inappropriate tool selection, opaque reasoning, and bias propagation-especially in high-stakes scenarios. To ensure responsible deployment, future development should prioritize controllability, interpretability, and robust oversight, aligning technological progress with ethical standards and societal values.
